newsitem.title: UK: DOLLAR/MARK UNDERMINED AS STERLING TUMBLES.
newsitem.headline: DOLLAR/MARK UNDERMINED AS STERLING TUMBLES.

text.p: The dollar ceded gains it had made against the mark earlier in Europe, as sterling tumbled, suffering its biggest losses against the German currency.

The pound slumped across the board, extending the slide triggered on Thursday after the Bank of England indicated it is not about to follow up yesterday's increase in interest rates anytime soon and that it wants the currency to fall.

While the pound fell 1.6 percent to set a 10-month low against the dollar, it lost more ground to the mark. This prompted dollar/mark to give back gains it had made earlier amid talk the Bundesbank may not nudge rates higher.

"The sterling bubble has well and truly burst," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro. "The cable decline looks a bit overstretched whereas sterling/mark looks like it could move down to 2.90. This is hitting dollar/mark a bit but it would have to go below 1.85 for it to look bad."

Sterling was at 2.9260/70 marks at 1034 GMT, down 4.5 percent from this week's highs and weaker than 2.9690/00 late Thursday in Europe. It was at $1.5692/02, down 3.5 percent since Wednesday and compared with $1.5880/90 yesterday.
The dollar was at 1.8675/79 marks from 1.8675/85 late Thursday. It was at 118.50/60 yen from 118.37/42 yesterday.
While pessimism about sterling's prospects is seen dominating New York activity, traders are expected to refocus on the outlook for German money-market rates.

Before its four-week summer recess, the Bundesbank signalled it could push up money-market rates if the mark extended its two-year slide against the dollar. But this has not deterred traders from driving the mark close to an eight-year low versus the dollar.
Dollar bulls expected Germany's fragile economy to prevent the Bundesbank from raising rates too high. This view was reinforced by Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke earlier on Friday.

Welteke said Germany's slow growth and high unemployment meant it was not appropriate to "turn the interest rate screw." He also said the Bundesbank should not raise rates as long as there were no signs of price pressures and that currency moves had so far had a limited impact on the German cost of living.
These comments overshadowed his remark the Bundesbank had already signalled the dollar/mark's correction was completed at 1.70 marks and lifted the U.S. currency against the mark.
"It is not a good time for a rate hike," said Stefan Schilbe, economist at Trinkaus & Burkhardt in Dusseldorf.
"They can move to a variable rate tender and change the repo rates by 10 or 20 basis points, but that will be all. And that won't have a long term impact on dollar/mark," he said.
Talk of a switch to a variable-rate tender is expected to be fanned before the German central bank announces terms of its repo rate next week.
Speculation the Bundesbank could intervene was also stoked when Welteke said the Bundesbank had no date for intervening in currency markets but was vlosely watching foreign exchange developments.
"Intervention might also be a possibility, but they will wait until the market gets ahead of itself," said Marian Bell, treasury economist at Royal Bank of Scotland.
The dollar also retreated against the yen. Concerns Japan's widening trade surplus with the U.S. will revive tensions between the two nations was seen capping dollar/yen's upside.
A report overnight showed Japan's June current account surplus leapt nearly 56 percent from a year ago while the trade surplus rose nearly 19 percent in the same period.
"I would expect nastier noises from the U.S. in the coming months, which will push the yen lower," said Bell.
-- Swaha Pattanaik, London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
